SATOM 3.4.0

SATOM mapped to the NAF Framework — the API describes itself and reads and writes desired state, configuration history, findings and metrics; a device that no longer matches its template is a finding; processes start from events, schedules and the API and can undo their own writes; SNMP polling and a syslog receiver; the Documentation Center on every node; CPU, memory and disk history of the nodes; the rest of the Wiki.

👤 ForOperatorAdministratorAdvanced user

Released: 2026-10-21 · All releases

In short#

SATOM is now mapped to the Network Automation Forum's reference framework — six functional blocks around the network infrastructure — and this release closes the gaps that mapping exposed. The REST API describes itself with an OpenAPI document and gains three families of endpoints: desired state (templates, bindings, baselines — read, and written with explicit capabilities), what SATOM has observed (configuration history and diffs, the current findings, a read-only metrics query) and processes. A device bound to a template that no longer matches it is a finding. Processes start from events, from a scheduled action and from the API, always as a rehearsal unless each door is armed, and a new Compensate step undoes what a walk wrote. Collection goes beyond the appliances' own APIs with SNMP v2c polling and a syslog receiver. Every node serves the Documentation Center itself, SATOM health keeps CPU, memory and disk history of both nodes, and the Wiki gains comments, following, export and Confluence publishing.

New#

Mapped to the NAF Framework#

  • Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework: the six blocks in SATOM's words, the five names that collide (the "Source of Truth" is the framework's Observability, not its Intent), and why SATOM aligns with it. The conformance matrix — every requirement, its state and the file that is the evidence — is published with the product documentation (docs/naf-alignment.html; on a node, /manual/docs/naf-alignment.html), pinned to the framework's commit da82b12, and a test derives from it the only verdict the documentation may state.

The API describes itself, and reads and writes intent and observations#

  • GET /api/v1/openapi.json — an OpenAPI 3.0 document built at request time from the live routes, the scope each one enforces and its summary. A route added tomorrow is documented the moment it is registered.
  • Intent: GET /templates, /templates/<id>, /bindings, /baselines, scoped to the token's ADOM like a console session. Writing needs two new explicit-only capabilities: template_draft creates templates, versions, bindings and baselines and never touches a device; template_apply approves (four-eyes, never the author) and pushes a template through the console's own path — a dry-run preview unless confirm is true, then the canary-first job behind the firmware gate. A token minted before this release cannot roll a template out. See REST API.
  • Observability: GET /appliances/<id>/config-history and config-diff over the Source of Truth, GET /findings, and GET /metrics/query, a read-only MetricsQL proxy that accepts SATOM's own satom_* series only, answers within 10 s or says so, and hands a product-bound token only its own devices' series. The metrics store itself stays on loopback; this route is the only way in from outside.

Intent deviation: a bound device that no longer matches its template is a finding#

  • The health engine's new Intent deviation check (on by default, its own toggle, sink family intent) renders each binding's template with the device's variables and compares it field by field with the cached device objects — the key-subset comparison the approval modal already uses, never equality against a raw snapshot, because an appliance fills in what the template never set. Measured on a FortiWeb 7.6.8 and an 8.0.6: the box answers "4" to a 4, counts its own sub-table rows and renumbers internal handles; those are ignored, and sub-table rows are reported unmeasured rather than guessed at.
  • One warning per binding, naming the fields that differ and never a value; maintenance and the drift exclude list silence it like drift. The bindings table shows the same verdict as a Compliance column, and hooks can subscribe to the typed event intent.deviation beside alert.fired. See Alerting and the Template library.

Processes start from events, on a schedule and from the API; Compensate undoes a walk#

  • A process can name a trigger event from the integration-hook catalogue, narrowed by ADOM, appliance, alert family and a severity floor. The walk is queued as a job the moment the event is noticed. Three rules bound a storm, each refusal kept as a run with status skipped: one running instance per process and appliance, a budget of runs per hour (default 10), and rehearsal unless Arm triggered walks is on — which the form says, in red, means SATOM writes with nobody at the screen.
  • Walk a process is a new action of the operator catalogue (rehearsal unless its armed parameter is on; an armed walk of a writing diagram runs only bound to a change request; flagged dangerous, so never through the generic actions API).
  • The Compensate step undoes what the walk wrote before it, newest first — only the steps that recorded an inverse (a status a catalogue action flipped, an Observatory fix, a provisioning run); a write with no inverse is named unknown, never guessed, and a failed write is never replayed.
  • GET /api/v1/processes, POST /api/v1/processes/<id>/run (rehearsal by default; "armed": true needs the new explicit process_arm capability) and GET /api/v1/process-runs/<id>. Every run records what started it.

Collection beyond the device APIs: SNMP polling and a syslog receiver#

  • A new snmp collector polls an appliance over SNMP v2c — uptime, the interface table with 64-bit byte counters, CPU, memory and disk from the vendor MIB (verified on FortiWeb 7.6.8; the other products' OIDs are the documented ones with HOST-RESOURCES as fallback) — on a client written on the standard library, so the offline bundles carry no new wheel. Opt-in per appliance: the edit form gains a switch, the port and the community, stored like the passwords and never shown again.
  • A syslog receiver (UDP and TCP; RFC 3164, RFC 5424 and the Fortinet key=value body) runs inside the scheduler on the primary, off by default, bound to 5514 unless told otherwise, and keeps only what known senders say; anything else is dropped and counted. Monitoring → Collection shows both, and (Global only) the last 500 messages with credential-shaped values blanked. SNMPv3, traps, flows and packet capture are out of scope and the manual says so. See Metrics collection.

Also in this release#

  • The manual on every node — /manual/ serves the Documentation Center and the generated reference pages from the node itself, readable without signing in and from the container image; the sign-in page's Documentation link and the user menu open it. See Documentation on the node.
  • Resource history of the SATOM nodes — Monitoring → SATOM health draws CPU, memory and disk of both nodes over 1 hour to 90 days with the limits from Settings → Thresholds; GET /api/v1/system/nodes and /system/nodes/history return the same readings. See Monitoring overview.
  • Wiki: comments, following, export and Confluence — threaded comments under published articles, following an article, topic, tag or ADOM with notices in the bell, Markdown and PDF export, and one-way publishing to a Confluence space with a credential scan that stops a publication naming a secret. See Wiki and Publishing to Confluence.

Changed#

  • Wiki groups are Administrator → Access → Groups, the same groups Python Studio apps are shared with: one list of teams instead of two that drift apart. The upgrade merges them and keeps every article's audience.
  • A FortiWeb template body may name its collection as the registry logical name, the cmdb tail or the full REST path; all three resolve to the same cached object.
  • Device findings and the alert.fired payload carry appliance_id, so a hook or a process trigger can address the device.

Fixed#

  • A SATOM node's disk read about 4 points emptier than it was. The percentage counted the space ext4 reserves for root, which PostgreSQL and SATOM cannot use. It is now df's figure, and the node tile shows used and free space. See Thresholds.
  • The SATOM nodes' CPU alert could never fire. Settings → Thresholds still held load-average limits (150 % / 400 %) for a reading that never goes above 100 %. The limits are now CPU busy 80 % / 95 %; a value saved under the old meaning is read as the default.
  • The Wiki list's page 2 and later kept only the first ticked ADOM of the filter.
  • One slow scheduled action no longer holds the whole scheduler tick. An Observatory scan whose sites sat behind a down host ran for almost eight minutes and delayed every other action, the metrics flush and the syslog journal with it. Observatory sites are now graded concurrently within a run budget (240 s by default), the deep-monitor sweep has its own budget (120 s), and a target the budget did not reach is recorded as unknown, never left on its previous grade. The scheduler log names any action that takes a minute or more.
  • satom get system health graded the disk with fixed limits (80 % / 90 %) while Settings → Thresholds said 80 % / 92 %. The CLI now reads the node's effective limits from /healthz and says so; when the node does not answer it falls back to the defaults and says that too.
  • The syslog receiver card says that enabling the receiver does not open the node's packet filter: allow the chosen port from the appliances' management networks on every node, primary and standby.
  • The offline installer on a bare Debian 12 container needed four workarounds, now fixed: the guided installer takes curl from the bundle instead of dying on "curl is missing"; only the packages the image lacks are installed and the base packages (systemd, udev, PAM, libc6) are never replaced, so the bundle's closure cannot break the base system; the database is created UTF8 on every image (a C-locale image gave SQL_ASCII and a misleading authentication hint); nginx is restarted after the vhost is written, so the install no longer ends with "does not accept connections on 443". The guided installer's --help no longer promises SETUP_EXISTING=update for a native install.
  • The documented upgrade path from 3.3.2 or older did not work as written — see Before you upgrade.

Before you upgrade#

  • Coming from 3.3.2 or older: apply satom-update-3.3.3.tar.gz (release v3.3.3) first, then this package. This package accepts only a node on 3.3.3 or newer. Install the 3.3.3 package's own update runner before applying it: the runner those nodes carry points pip at a staging directory only root can read, so the apply fails at pip install and rolls back — every time, with the data intact (measured on a 2.11.0 node). As root, after the console's preflight has verified the package: extract deploy/ from the package's app.tar.gz into a root-only directory and run SATOM_DEPLOY_SRC=<that dir>/deploy bash <that dir>/deploy/install-runner.sh; then apply the package from Software Update as usual. The exact commands are in the update manual (docs/offline-update-packages.md §3) of the product tree. A node on 3.3.3 or newer never needs this step.
  • Installing 3.4.0 from an offline bundle on a bare container image works without the four workarounds the 2.11.0 bundle needed (curl from the bundle, base packages never replaced, UTF8 database, nginx restarted after the vhost) — see Fixed.
  • Database changes: the upgrade runs migrations wiki04 (Wiki groups merged into Access → Groups), wiki05 (comments and subscriptions), wiki06 (Confluence spaces and pages), orch01 (process triggers and the key a run was started by) and coll01 (SNMP fields on appliances). Nothing existing is removed.
  • New default-on check: Intent deviation starts evaluating at the next alert run. A fleet with bindings that were never applied will see one warning per such binding — that is the finding working; apply the template or unbind, or switch the check off under Settings → Email & Alerts.
  • Nothing listens by default: the syslog receiver is off and SNMP is off on every appliance until you enable them.
  • API tokens: existing tokens keep exactly what they had. The template write and process-arming endpoints need the new explicit capabilities on a token; nothing is granted retroactively.
